author: Abbey Mulcahy
title: Cats, women and inescapable loneliness: 'Nothing's About to Happen to Me' album review - The Minnesota Daily
text:
When it comes to cry-in-the-shower music, Mitski’s songs are often a top pick. Her newest album, however, departs from her typical tear-jerking artistry for a restrained and sonically layered examination of old histories, new beginnings and loneliness.
Mitski Miyawaki, known professionally as Mitski, is a Japanese-American indie rock artist known for her heartbreaking yet beautiful songs. She released her first album, “Lush,” in 2012.
Released Feb. 27, “Nothing’s About to Happen to Me” marks Mitski’s eighth studio album and her first full release in three years.
It’s a relatively quick listen, totaling 34 minutes, but each song carries weight and prompts listeners to consider their own relationship with loneliness. It’s enjoyable and undeniably familiar.
Its 11 songs depict a narrator suspended in rumination. She croons about cats who comfort her broken heart, asks if she’d be more lovable as a dead woman and speaks of death and misery as though they were old friends.
She’s torn between clinging to the past and fleeing it, longing to stay with her absent lover forever while also entertaining visions of big cities where these memories can’t follow. Confusion and subtle mania haunt the lyricism, presenting a Mitski that’s less volatile than usual, but still just as in touch with her feelings.
The album features live instrumentation by the ensemble touring group that accompanied her 2023 album, “The Land Is Inhospitable and So Are We.” Her newest album continues the sonic exploration she started in the previous album.
In “Charon’s Obol” — named after the coin placed in or on the mouth of a dead person before burial in ancient Greek and Roman traditions — a frontier-esque guitar twangs in the background, complementing cowboy hums and fiddle riffs.
The opening song, “In a Lake,” begins hypnotically with a banjo strum, but it’s eventually hijacked by a trumpet outburst, honking cars and emergency sirens, throwing the listener into the familiar chaos of a city.
Throughout both songs, Mitski’s voice maintains a steady connection with the listener.
She dropped two songs as singles prior to the album release, “Where’s My Phone?” and “I’ll Change for You,” and they remain standouts even after the others have been unveiled.
“Where’s My Phone?” has a soft rock sound reminiscent of earlier Mitski albums. It pushes forward with an urgency, interspersing the mundane question of, “Where’s my phone?” with musing, “Where’d I go?” While it’s overtly comedic, exemplified by a censor that bleeps out of Mitski’s profanity, there’s a sense of quiet desperation throughout.
The second single, “I’ll Change for You,” is smooth and classical, mixed with clinking glasses and laughter. The human flourishes make it feel like a scene from a movie.
Several songs nod to Mitski’s foray into the theater scene. Human flourishes — be they the voices in “I’ll Change for You” or the cityscape in “In a Lake” — give listeners insight into the music she’s creating for the stage adaptation of “The Queen’s Gambit.” Her participation in the project was announced in 2023.
The instrumentation varies across the album, oscillating between almost-country, rock and ballad, but the lyrics reveal common sentiments: loneliness and a fascination with death.
“Instead of here, I’m where nobody can reach,” Mitski sings in “Instead of Here,” shortly followed by “I’m nobody’s anyone anymore” two songs later in “Rules.” She doesn’t seem angered or devastated, simply accepting these feelings as fact.
Ultimately, “Nothing’s About to Happen to Me” is the perfect balance of melancholy and restraint. It holds a mirror to Mitski’s inner world, letting her unfaltering voice lead listeners through relatable feelings of loneliness, nostalgia and desperation without the soul-crushing sadness that much of her other music has.
